Figure 2: Hetero-model training data splits. Training data (n=103) distributions for the three different experimental setups (subject count on x-axis). Training split 1 has all four modalities for all subjects. Training split 2 has all four modalities for only 11 subjects, with the remaining subjects each having only a single modality (23 with T1w, 23 with T2w, 23 with FLAIR, and 23 with DWI). Training split 3 has T1w scans for all 103 subjects and each subject also has one addition sequence (34 with T2w, 34 with FLAIR, and 35 with DWI).

Figure 3: Multimodal Attention Router (MMAR)-based architecture. A) Overview of the multi-encoder, shared-decoder model (showing highest (F 0) and lowest (FL) resolution levels for one encoder). MMAR blocks fuse features from each modality encoder prior to decoding. B) Detailed MMAR block illustrating fusion with one missing and three available modalities. Available features are normalised then patchified via a shared convolution and injected with positional and modality embeddings. Following processing by windowed self-attention transformer blocks, features are reshaped to their original dimensions. Finally, a softmax operation across the modality dimension generates spatial- and channel-wise attention maps, which are used to fuse the features via elementwise multiplication. 10
Figure 4: Dropout and corruption augmentation. Data augmentation applied to batches of T1w, T2w, FLAIR, and DWI (left to right) MRI scans during training (for the corruption-based experiments).
